prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms brought time-keeping to the 10^-18 level and opened new tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: a single prize part for the optical lattice clock, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. After the first round I can say more precisely why I hold it. The new idea is the magic wavelength. A lattice at that wavelength shifts the two clock levels equally, so the atoms can be held still, free of Doppler and recoil shifts, and thousands of them can be interrogated together. That is a physical insight about the atom, and neither the frequency comb (2005) nor ion control (2012) contains it. Everything later follows from it: stability and accuracy near 1e-18, redshift across millimetres, bounds on drifting constants and clock comparisons between continents. What persuades me most is that the performance has been reproduced and cross-checked by independent laboratories (RIKEN and Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL). Clock-to-clock agreement is the quantitative theory-experiment type of test I trust, and it does not rest on a single measurement. The maturity is real, because the result is measured and not projected. Two names also fit comfortably inside the statutory limit of three. Five members have now independently reached the same configuration, but I rest my judgment on the physics and not on the count.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is overlap. Ye shares the 2005 prize, Wineland the 2012 prize, and a sceptic can call this a third chapter of precision metrology and the same laureate twice. The pending redefinition of the second is still a loose end. Danielsson's question is also fair: so far the fundamental tests (redshift, constants, dark-matter couplings) give null results, so what we have learned about nature is a very precise confirmation, not a surprise. I do not think any of this is decisive, but I do not want to pretend it is absent. In the end the committee must decide whether it values a measurement instrument that opens a new regime as highly as the discovery of a new phenomenon. If it does not, B016 or B013 would be the more natural choice.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers the Higgs discovery (B046), values attribution cleanliness in B053 but asks what has actually been learned about nature, since the redshift and constants tests are null results and the clock follows the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I accept the question, and it is the right one for me to answer. A null result at 1e-18 is not empty: it is a bound on how much a constant can drift or how any couplings of dark matter to atoms can behave, and the redshift measurement across a millimetre is a positive observation of general relativity at a scale nobody could reach before. The claim of discovery in the citation concerns the magic-wavelength lattice itself, which is something found about atoms, and I would keep the wording on that. I also understand that the Higgs is the more famous result. But your own case_against says that four names with strong claims make any trio arbitrary, and the Higgs experiments are tied to collaborations of thousands. I cannot judge that allocation from atomic physics, and I do not think a prize with an arbitrary trio is better than one with a clean pair. I thank you for saying you would move toward B053 if the allocation cannot be settled.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice-clock step is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, that performance is already confirmed and that the pending redefinition of the second is a downstream consequence and not a reason to wait.
responses.response: I agree and I have moved a little toward you on timing. In round 1 I called the redefinition a qualification; after reading you, Johansson and Pearce I think I was wrong to treat it as one. The evidence for the prize is the demonstrated performance and the cross-laboratory comparisons, and the redefinition is a metrological decision that follows that evidence, so it affects the citation wording and not the date. I would keep the point you make in your own citation, the magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms, because it separates the result from the comb and ion-clock prizes. I note your JILA lineage with Hall; Ye is at JILA, so your disclosure is appropriate, and I do not think it changes the science.

responses.point: Olsson prefers aberration-corrected electron microscopy (B052) as an invention in the statutory sense and presses the reservation that the lattice clock is incremental after combs and ion clocks.
responses.response: I have thought about the statutory word invention again, because it applies equally to the clock: Katori proposed and realised a new clock architecture. So the invention argument does not separate B052 from B053. What separates them for me is that sub-angstrom imaging is an enabling tool whose physics comes from what others then do with it, while the lattice clock is both the instrument and the physics test, since the clock itself measures redshift and constants. I also share your worry about the STEM corrector of Krivanek, Dellby and Lupini, which leaves the TEM credit incomplete. You have been open about your own closeness to the field, and I think that was the right thing to do. If the expert report resolves the STEM priority I would regard B052 more favourably, but I would still not put it ahead of the clock.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect (B013) for a general Z2 mechanism and fifteen years of independent confirmation, and lists B053 as an alternative.
responses.response: I find the mechanism a beautiful and general one, and I have therefore changed my second alternative from B001 to B013: it is the candidate that I would most want to see recognised if the clock fails. The obstacle remains attribution. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe realisation, and Kane, Mele, Molenkamp and Hasan, but not these, would be named; the members do not agree on the triple, and I do not know how the 2016 prize bears on this because I defer to you and Eriksson on condensed matter. If the expert report gave a defensible triple and made the overlap with the 2016 prize clear, I would consider whether the physical interest of a new state of matter outweighs the interest of a new measurement instrument. As things stand it does not yet beat a clean two-name credit on the same grounds of maturity.

responses.point: Pearce, as Chair, moved the clock to first place but insists that the Sr-lattice priority question is not closed on the committee's say-so and needs an expert report on SYRTE, PTB and NIST before names are fixed.
responses.response: I agree and I think my own round-1 sentence was too soft. As far as I recall, Katori's proposal in 2001 and the first strontium lattice clock work at Tokyo and then JILA are the core, and the early groups in Paris and Braunschweig reached comparable results at much the same time, with contributions from Lemonde, Ludlow and others in accuracy. I hold the pair of Katori and Ye with some confidence because the concept and the record-accuracy programme map onto those two, and I do not think the other groups' contributions were the invention. But I accept that I recall this from memory, and I support an expert report that tests it before the citation is fixed. If the report shows another early contributor with a claim comparable to Ye's, I would reopen the choice of names, though not the choice of candidate.

uncertainties: Whether the expert report on the Sr-lattice priority history confirms Katori and Ye as the right and sufficient pair, or shows another early group with a comparable claim.
Whether the committee weighs a third precision-metrology prize (after 2005 and 2012, with Ye as a repeat laureate) as a step too far, which I judge the main real risk to B053.
Whether the B013 attribution can be given an agreed triple, which would make it the strongest competing configuration in my view.
How the committee values an instrument that opens a new regime against the discovery of a phenomenon, a question on which colleagues disagree and on which I have a view but no proof.
statement.conflict_note: No formal recusal is required for B053, and I am unaware of any personal tie to Katori or Ye. I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund attosecond group and with Ursula Keller's group; this is close to the attosecond theme but not to any shortlisted candidate. I continue to take care on the atomic, molecular and optical entries (B016, B001), where my professional proximity is greatest, and my alternatives should be read with that in mind. My colleague Kroll has disclosed a lineage tie to JILA that I note; it does not alter my view of the science.
